foundation.title: Foundation of self-knowledge
foundation.description: Six steps — one for each Foundation area: values, meaning, personality, emotions, relationships and life balance. At the end you build your profile.
foundation.finaleDescription: Every area is covered — you can now build your psychological profile.

step1.intro: Discover what truly matters to you — the axis the rest of the profile is built around.

step2.intro: Transformative purpose: name the direction that gives your actions meaning.

step3.intro: A short Big Five measure — a map of your personality traits.

step4.intro: Emotion regulation (ERQ): check how you usually handle emotions.

step5.intro: Attachment style (ECR-RS): look at your patterns in close relationships.

step6.intro: Wheel of Life: rate the balance of your life areas and close the Foundation.

anger-signal.title: Anger as a Signal
anger-signal.description: Six weeks: noticing, a pause, another perspective, what matters, a choice of your own and what stays. Work with your own situations at your own pace. Eight weeks after the end the path invites you to a Return. If anger leads to violence or someone feels unsafe around you, this path is not enough — seek professional support.

reflection.severity: How much did anger get in the way this week?

w1.title: Noticing
w1.why: Name the anger: how it arrives, how it usually reacts and what you want to change.
w1.question: What helped you recognise tension building?

w2.title: The pause
w2.why: Prepare one small action for when tension starts to rise, and check what a thought adds.
w2.question: What helped you pause, even briefly?

w3.title: Another perspective
w3.why: Separate what happened from your first interpretation. Halfway: we check the dose, not the result.
w3.question: Which thought gave you more room to choose?

w4.title: What matters
w4.why: Listen for what this anger defends and find words for the need or boundary.
w4.question: What need or boundary could you name?

w5.title: A choice of your own
w5.why: Try one change in a safe, everyday situation.
w5.question: What did the attempt show, even if the conversation did not go your way?

w6.title: What stays
w6.why: Keep what helps and write yourself a letter for a worse day.
w6.question: What would you like to return to when anger rises again?

return.title: The return
return.why: Eight weeks after the end: what stayed, what came back.
return.question: What from this path stayed with you day to day?

step1.title: A starting point
step1.intro: Notice how anger affects your days. This barometer is an informal guide; you will return to it halfway, at the end and at the Return.
step1.why: Without a starting point you cannot see change. This measure is your reference for the whole way.

step2.title: How anger arrives
step2.intro: Look at one recent situation: what came before it, what happened in your body and how anger usually reacts.
step2.why: Anger is easier to notice when you know its signals and your typical reactions. The map gives names to what used to happen on its own.

step3.title: How I will know it works
step3.intro: Say in your own words what you most want to change and how you will know it is working. The sentence stays at the top of the path.
step3.why: A goal in your own words holds the direction for six weeks and tells you how you will know the path works.

step4.title: My pause plan
step4.intro: Choose an early signal and one doable action. Include how you will return to the conversation when it is safe.
step4.why: In the moment of anger there is no time to invent anything. A ready “if…, then…” does it for you.

step5.title: Fact or interpretation
step5.intro: Take one thought that fuels anger. See which part is an observation and which is an assumption.
step5.why: Anger grows not only from the situation but from what you add to it. A named assumption loses some of its force.

step6.title: A thought that gives choice
step6.intro: Return to a saved moment. Find a fairer thought that respects both the facts and your boundaries.
step6.why: A fairer thought does not make you agree. It leaves you a choice of how to react.

step7.title: The barometer halfway
step7.intro: Repeat the barometer. See in Progress whether anything moved, without judging yourself by the score.
step7.why: A measure halfway shows the direction before the path ends. Sometimes it is what says it is worth staying with what already works.

step8.title: Is it too much?
step8.intro: Say honestly how many of the practices you really do. The path proposes a calmer rhythm if needed.
step8.why: People drop out of paths not because they do too little, but because the path looks disappointed. There is none of that here.

step9.title: Listening to anger
step9.intro: Choose a moment you can comfortably revisit. If the language of parts fits, treat anger as a voice you can listen to.
step9.why: Anger that someone has listened to does not need to shout. The trailhead is the first such conversation.

step10.title: What it tries to protect
step10.intro: Explore this part’s intention. Understanding it does not mean agreeing with hurtful behaviour.
step10.why: A protector that knows you understand it hands over the wheel more easily than one you fight.

step11.title: A need and a request
step11.intro: Return to a saved moment. Name what matters and form a request or boundary you can express calmly.
step11.why: Anger usually defends a need. A request says directly what the outburst said indirectly.

step12.title: One possible change
step12.intro: Choose a recurring difficulty and a small step within your control.
step12.why: Rumination keeps anger going; one step on the matter releases it. Influence counts, not size.

step13.title: Trying another way
step13.intro: Test one prediction, such as “no one will hear a calm request”. Choose a safe situation and see what happens.
step13.why: A prediction tested in life teaches more than ten rounds of thinking. The result need not be good to be valuable.

step14.title: Kind and accountable
step14.intro: If you wish, write to yourself after a difficult moment. Make room for kindness and responsibility for a specific action.
step14.why: The letter breaks the loop outburst → shame → tension → outburst. Kindness does not excuse repair; it makes it possible.

step15.title: The barometer at the end
step15.intro: Repeat the barometer and compare your results in Progress. Notice small changes the score may not capture, too.
step15.why: Two points on a track are a picture of change over time, not a verdict. The rest is in Moments.

step16.title: A letter for a worse day
step16.intro: Write to the you of the future: what you already know, what helped, what to do in the first minute of anger. It returns in the week you choose.
step16.why: A worse day will come. A letter read weeks later works like the voice of someone who knows you and is on your side.

step17.title: What I take with me
step17.intro: Choose a helpful practice, a signal to pause and a way to seek support. You do not need to keep everything.
step17.why: What stays in the week’s rhythm lasts after the path. This step closes the path and sets the repeats.

step18.title: The barometer eight weeks on
step18.intro: Eight weeks after the end: repeat the barometer and see what stayed.
step18.why: A habit is measured in weeks, not days. This measure says whether the change stayed.

step19.title: The return
step19.intro: Read your letter, mark what stayed and choose one small move for the coming week.
step19.why: The return is not an exam. It is the moment you can resume what helped before the old reaction settles back in.

paced-breathing.intro: A few comfortable breaths, without forcing the rhythm. Stop if it feels unpleasant.

moment-anger.intro: Five taps: what took the wheel, when noticed, what instead, how strong. No need to wait for an outburst or catch up on empty days.

noticeSigns.title: Notice a signal in your body
noticeSigns.why: Noticing and naming is enough. A note in Moments can help you return to the moment.

noticeCost.title: Notice what came after the reaction
noticeCost.why: Without judging. Seeing the effect shows what changing the reaction is for.

pauseInConversation.title: Try your pause
pauseInConversation.why: Even a short one. Tick it in Moments, even if it came late.

announceReturn.title: Announce the break and the return
announceReturn.why: The other person accepts a pause more easily when they know you will come back.

breathBefore.title: Take a breath before you answer
breathBefore.why: One longer exhale gives the body the second the thought needs.

altThought.title: Recall another thought
altThought.why: See whether it gives you a little more choice.

factOnly.title: Say just the fact, without the addition
factOnly.why: Facts without judgements are easier to hear and harder to argue with.

requestNotReproach.title: Name a need or boundary
requestNotReproach.why: You can ask for a change without a guarantee that the other person will agree.

nameNeed.title: Name the need in your head
nameNeed.why: You do not have to say it yet. A named need turns anger into information.

returnToTalk.title: Return to the conversation after the pause
returnToTalk.why: The return matters more than the pause. It teaches that a break is not an escape.

applySolution.title: Take one small step
applySolution.why: Choose an action within your control.

calmRequest.title: Try a calm request
calmRequest.why: Notice the response without judging yourself by the outcome.

sayNoCalmly.title: Say “no” without raising your voice
sayNoCalmly.why: A boundary spoken calmly is a boundary. It does not need force.

repairRelationship.title: Make room for repair
repairRelationship.why: If it is safe, acknowledge a specific action and offer repair. The other person may need time.

keepPause.title: Stay with your pause
keepPause.why: Three times a week is enough for the move to outlast the path.

anger-signal.goal: Notice anger earlier, make room for a pause and express what matters without hurting yourself or others.

anxiety-approach.title: Anxiety: Approach Instead of Avoid
anxiety-approach.description: Eight weeks with worry and avoidance: your own map, examining thoughts, small everyday attempts and what stays. Set your own pace. Eight weeks after the end the path invites you to a Return. This path does not replace support for panic attacks, OCD, trauma or a crisis.

reflection.severity: How much did anxiety and worry limit this week?

w1.title: Noticing
w1.why: Name the anxiety: the situations, the body, what it makes you do and what you want to return to.
w1.question: What could you notice before the urge to withdraw?

w2.title: A worry or a task
w2.why: Postpone worries to a fixed time and sort which are a problem and which a hypothesis.
w2.question: Which worry turned out to be a task, and which a hypothesis?

w3.title: Another perspective
w3.why: Notice the difference between a prediction and what is already known, and test one prediction in life.
w3.question: Which thought gave you more room to choose?

w4.title: Within my reach
w4.why: Turn one worry into a doable step. Halfway: we check the dose, not the result.
w4.question: What step was within your reach, and which unknown could you leave?

w5.title: A small approach
w5.why: Build the ladder and return to a safe situation in a manageable dose.
w5.question: What did the attempt show, regardless of your anxiety level?

w6.title: Back to the attempt
w6.why: The same ladder, a second time. A repeat or a smaller step is progress too.
w6.question: What was different the second time?

w7.title: What matters
w7.why: Choose a helpful way to return to life. You can skip these steps.
w7.question: What meaningful thing found some room alongside anxiety?

w8.title: What stays
w8.why: Keep what helps and write yourself a letter for a worse day.
w8.question: What small practice would you like to return to?

return.title: The return
return.why: Eight weeks after the end: what stayed, what came back.
return.question: What from this path stayed with you day to day?

step1.title: A starting point
step1.intro: Notice how anxiety affects your days. This score is a reference point, not a diagnosis. You will return to it halfway, at the end and at the Return.
step1.why: Without a starting point you cannot see change. This measure is your reference for the whole way.

step2.title: Living with unknowns
step2.intro: If you wish, explore your response to uncertainty. You can skip this measure; it returns at the end.
step2.why: Intolerance of uncertainty keeps worry going. Measured at the start and the end, it shows whether room for the unknown is growing.

step3.title: My anxiety map
step3.intro: Name one situation, what anxiety makes you do and what you want to return to. The map will be available under “My plan”.
step3.why: Anxiety is easier to notice when you know its situations and your typical moves. The map gives names to what used to happen on its own.

step4.title: How I will know it works
step4.intro: Say in your own words what you most want to change and how you will know it is working. The sentence stays at the top of the path.
step4.why: A goal in your own words holds the direction for eight weeks and tells you how you will know the path works.

step5.title: A worry or a task
step5.intro: See whether there is something you can do now, or whether the thought concerns what might happen.
step5.why: The worry tree separates a problem from a hypothesis. The problem gets a step; the hypothesis can wait for worry time.

step6.title: What anxiety adds
step6.intro: Look at one concern. Notice assumptions and generalisations without criticising yourself for having them.
step6.why: A named assumption loses some of its force. This is not about thinking positively, only about seeing what is known.

step7.title: A thought that makes room
step7.intro: Return to a saved moment. Check the facts and find a fairer thought — it does not need to promise everything will go well.
step7.why: A fairer thought makes room for uncertainty instead of removing it. That is enough to approach.

step8.title: A small uncertainty experiment
step8.intro: Return to a saved moment and its prediction. Choose a safe, minor situation and one unnecessary check; see what happens.
step8.why: Anxiety predicts. One tested forecast teaches more than ten reassurances.

step9.title: One step within reach
step9.intro: Take a worry you can act on. Explore options and choose one doable step.
step9.why: A worry that gets a step stops circling. Influence counts, not size.

step10.title: The measure halfway
step10.intro: Repeat the measure. See in Progress whether anything moved, without judging yourself by the score.
step10.why: A measure halfway shows the direction before the path ends. Sometimes it is what says it is worth staying with what already works.

step11.title: Is it too much?
step11.intro: Say honestly how many of the practices you really do. The path proposes a calmer rhythm if needed.
step11.why: People drop out of paths not because they do too little, but because the path looks disappointed. There is none of that here.

step12.title: My ladder of small attempts
step12.intro: Arrange a few safe situations from easier to harder. Begin with a small attempt and keep genuine safety precautions.
step12.why: Approaching in a small dose teaches that it can be borne and that the prediction does not come true. A drop in anxiety is not the goal of the attempt.

step13.title: Returning to my attempt
step13.intro: Open the same ladder. Look at what your attempts teach you and choose a repeat or a smaller step. You do not have to move up yet.
step13.why: The second attempt teaches more than the first: that is when you see what changes and what does not.

step14.title: Another stance towards a symptom
step14.intro: An optional change of stance towards a familiar, mild symptom. Do not induce breathlessness or other concerning sensations. If unsure, skip this step and discuss it with a professional.
step14.why: Fear of a symptom keeps the symptom going. Inviting it with humour takes its power away.

step15.title: Attention on what I am doing
step15.intro: If you wish, shift attention from monitoring yourself to the activity at hand. Anxiety does not need to disappear first.
step15.why: Monitoring yourself turns anxiety up. Attention on the activity leaves it in the background, where it fades on its own.

step16.title: Room for something meaningful
step16.intro: Optionally plan one small activity that matters to you. Adjust it to what is manageable today.
step16.why: The life you return to is the reason for all this work. One meaningful thing a week is enough to feel it.

step17.title: The measure at the end
step17.intro: Repeat the measure and compare results in Progress. Also notice what you could return to, even with anxiety present.
step17.why: Two points on a track are a picture of change over time, not a verdict. The rest is in Moments and on the ladder.

step18.title: Unknowns at the end
step18.intro: If you wish, repeat the intolerance-of-uncertainty measure and compare it with the start.
step18.why: Room for the unknown is the aim of this path. This measure says whether it grew.

step19.title: A letter for a worse day
step19.intro: Write to the you of the future: what you already know, what helped, what to do in the first minute of anxiety. It returns in the week you choose.
step19.why: A worse day will come. A letter read weeks later works like the voice of someone who knows you and is on your side.

step20.title: What I take with me
step20.intro: Choose a helpful practice, a small attempt to repeat and a way to seek support. You do not need to keep everything.
step20.why: What stays in the week’s rhythm lasts after the path. This step closes the path and sets the repeats.

step21.title: The measure eight weeks on
step21.intro: Eight weeks after the end: repeat the measure and see what stayed.
step21.why: A habit is measured in weeks, not days. This measure says whether the change stayed.

step22.title: The return
step22.intro: Read your letter, mark what stayed and choose one small move for the coming week.
step22.why: The return is not an exam. It is the moment you can resume what helped before avoidance settles back in.

paced-breathing.intro: Breathe at a comfortable pace without forcing it. This offers support; it is not a condition for taking action.

moment-anxiety.intro: Five taps: what pulled, when noticed, what instead, how strong. No need to wait for a hard day or catch up on empty ones.

worry-postponement.intro: Choose a brief, regular time, away from bedtime. During the day, note a worry and try returning to what you are doing.

noticeAvoidance.title: Notice a moment of withdrawal
noticeAvoidance.why: Name it in Moments without judging yourself.

noticeUrge.title: Notice the urge to check
noticeUrge.why: Just noticing, before you check. You do not have to give it up yet.

postponeWorry.title: Postpone a worry to your worry time
postponeWorry.why: Every worry time counts a day. Three a week is enough.

sortWorry.title: A worry or a task?
sortWorry.why: With one worry, ask: is there a step within my reach? If so, write it down.

predictionCheck.title: Compare the worry with what happened
predictionCheck.why: Note a prediction beforehand and an observation afterwards.

uncertainDecisions.title: Leave a small unknown
uncertainDecisions.why: Choose a minor decision without real risk, such as a film without another review.

firstStep.title: Take one doable step
firstStep.why: Choose an action within your control.

leaveOneUnknown.title: Do not check a second time
leaveOneUnknown.why: One check is enough. Notice what happens to the anxiety without the second.

exposureLow.title: Try an easy rung
exposureLow.why: Record what happened. A drop in anxiety is not the only sign of learning.

stayAMinute.title: Stay a minute longer
stayAMinute.why: In a situation you would like to leave. A minute is enough.

exposureNext.title: Repeat or adjust an attempt
exposureNext.why: You can stay on the same rung, make it smaller or choose the next one.

doItAnyway.title: Do it anyway
doItAnyway.why: One thing from the map you want to return to. Anxiety may come along.

meaningfulAct.title: Do one small meaningful thing
meaningfulAct.why: Choose something that matters even when anxiety comes along.

attentionOut.title: Attention on the activity, not on yourself
attentionOut.why: When you notice monitoring yourself, return to what you are doing. Twice a week.

planApproach.title: Plan another small attempt
planApproach.why: Choose a realistic time and scale you would like to return to.

keepWorryTime.title: Stay with your worry time
keepWorryTime.why: Three times a week is enough for the practice to outlast the path.

anxiety-approach.goal: Make room for uncertainty and take small steps towards what matters, even with anxiety present.

mapLabels.withoutFear: What I want to return to

shame-compassion.title: From shame to compassion
shame-compassion.description: Eight weeks of work with shame, based on compassion-focused therapy and the language of parts (IFS). The goal: to notice shame sooner, to answer it with warmth instead of attacking yourself, attacking others or hiding, and to come back into contact. First you recognise which parts take the wheel and build a place you can return to. Then the compassionate side of yourself, a plan for the hot moment and the question what this shame is about. Next you meet the critic as a part, write a letter and learn a voice that takes your side, and in the last weeks you come out of hiding in small, safe steps. Alongside the steps: breath, Moments and short practices, one real-life task a week, a dose check halfway, and a Return eight weeks after the end. This path is no substitute for therapy when shame is tied to violence, abuse or a serious crisis.

reflection.severity: How much did shame affect this week?

w1.title: Recognise
w1.why: Name shame and its parts before we start answering.
w1.question: In which situations did shame show up most, and which part took the wheel?

w2.title: The compassionate side
w2.why: A place, an image and a self you can come back to.

question.m: How did your body react when you turned to yourself with warmth? What did the resistance say?
question.f: How did your body react when you turned to yourself with warmth? What did the resistance say?

w3.title: The response
w3.why: A plan for the hot moment and the question what this shame is about.

question.m: When did you use your shame response, and when did a part get there first?
question.f: When did you use your shame response, and when did a part get there first?

w4.title: Look differently
w4.why: Evidence through the eyes of someone close. Halfway: we check the dose, not the result.

question.m: Which moments of the week turned out to be a demand, not a deed?
question.f: Which moments of the week turned out to be a demand, not a deed?

w5.title: The critic as a part
w5.why: Learn what it protects and take the wheel from it.
w5.question: What was the critic trying to protect this week?

w6.title: A new voice
w6.why: A letter to yourself and the sentence you defend yourself with.
w6.question: When did your defending voice speak up, and when was it missed most?

w7.title: Out of hiding
w7.why: Check in life what happens when you are seen.

question.m: What happened when you showed up as you are?
question.f: What happened when you showed up as you are?

w8.title: Make it last
w8.why: What stays with me and a letter for a worse day.
w8.question: How will you know shame is taking the wheel again, and what will you do then?

return.title: The return
return.why: Eight weeks after the end: what stayed, what came back.
return.question: What from this path stayed with you day to day?

step1.intro: Start by measuring self-compassion. The same scale returns halfway, at the end and at the Return.
step1.title: Self-compassion
step1.why: Without a starting point you cannot see change. This measure is your reference for the whole way.

step2.intro: A second measure: the three voices you answer yourself with when things go wrong. It returns at the end and at the Return.
step2.title: Three voices
step2.why: Shame is kept alive by three inner voices. Once you measure them, you know which one needs the work most.

step3.intro: See where shame speaks up most, how you react to it and which demand on yourself sits behind it. The reactions become parts in your registry.
step3.why: Shame is easier to notice when you know its places and your usual reactions. The map names what used to just happen.

step4.intro: Say in your own words what you most want to change and how you'll know it's working. That sentence stays at the top of the path.
step4.title: How I will know it changed
step4.why: Your own sense of the goal keeps the direction for eight weeks and tells you how you will know the path is working.

step5.intro: Before you turn to yourself with warmth, build a place to return to when it gets too much, and name what your resistance says.
step5.why: Warmth toward yourself can be hard. You need a place to come back to when it gets too much.

step6.intro: Create an image of a compassionate figure, starting with someone you find easy to care for. Its sentence returns in the following steps.
step6.title: Compassionate figure
step6.why: It is easier to receive warmth from a figure than to raise it in yourself from nothing. Its words will return in the next steps.

step7.intro: Now you are the compassion. Posture, voice, the eight qualities of Self-energy and a sentence to the part that is ashamed.
step7.why: The figure was a bridge. Now you learn to sound warm yourself toward the part that feels shame.

step8.intro: Build a personal plan for the moment of shame: signal, breath, an unblending sentence, one question, one sentence and a small move towards contact. From now on you practise it in life.
step8.title: Plan for a hard moment
step8.why: In the moment of shame there is no time to think. A ready plan lets your response get ahead of the part.

step9.intro: Take one moment from Moments and ask what the shame is about. A deed can be repaired, an event needs care, a demand needs checking.
step9.why: A deed, an event and a demand each need a different response. Without this question you treat them all the same.

step10.intro: Pick a moment and take apart the hot "I am…" thought. Look for evidence through the eyes of someone close to you, not a prosecutor.
step10.title: Thought record
step10.why: The hot thought “I am…” sounds like a fact. Laid out as evidence it loses its force.

step11.intro: Halfway: repeat the self-compassion scale. A picture of change, not a verdict.
step11.title: Self-compassion — halfway
step11.why: The second point shows the direction before you reach the end. It is a picture, not a grade.

step12.intro: Let's check the dose, not the result. If there are too many practices, fewer will stay; if you're doing none, the smallest one stays.
step12.title: Is it too much?
step12.why: The path has to fit into life. Better less and regular than a lot and never.

step13.intro: Pick a moment when the critic spoke up and treat it as a trailhead to the part. Enter from the position of your compassionate self.
step13.title: Trailhead
step13.why: The Critic shows up in concrete moments. One of them is the door to a conversation with that part.

step14.intro: Get to know the Critic as a protector: what is it afraid would happen if it stopped? At the end write the sentence with which you take the wheel from it.
step14.title: What the Critic guards
step14.why: The Critic is not an enemy but a protection that grew out of fear. Once you know what it guards, you can take the wheel from it.

step15.intro: Optional step. Talk to the Critic directly: the assistant plays its voice and you answer from Self.
step15.title: A talk with the Critic
step15.why: Some find it easier to hear a part when it has a voice of its own. Skip this if it does not feel like your way.

step16.intro: Pick a moment and write a letter to yourself in the voice of your compassionate self. At the end you'll check that the letter holds support, not advice.
step16.title: Letter to myself
step16.why: Writing slows the compassionate self's voice down enough to leave something you can return to.

step17.intro: The fierce side of compassion: how a friend would defend you and the sentence you defend yourself with, without "sorry" and without "but".
step17.title: In my own defence
step17.why: Compassion is also firmness. A defending sentence said once is easier in a real situation.

step18.intro: Move from the demand to a belief about yourself. The fair demand from "What is this shame about?" becomes the alternative belief you now collect evidence for.
step18.title: What I think of myself
step18.why: Under a demand sits a belief about yourself. A new belief needs evidence, which you collect from now on.

step19.intro: Test in life the prediction "if they see the real me, they'll reject me". A small, safe situation, the prediction written down, then the result.
step19.title: Testing it in life
step19.why: The prediction “they will reject me” is only tested in the world. A small situation gives proof that rehearsing in your head cannot.

step20.intro: Optional step, only if the protectors agree. Stay with a younger part for a while, without fixing. "Not yet" is a good answer too and completes the step.
step20.title: With the younger part
step20.why: Shame often has an old source. Being with it without fixing changes more than arguments — only with the consent of the parts that protect.

step21.intro: Repeat the self-compassion scale. You'll see the series: start, halfway, end.
step21.title: Self-compassion — at the end
step21.why: The third point closes the picture: start, middle, end. It is your proof of change.

step22.intro: Repeat the three-voices scale. The reassured self grows, the inadequate and hated selves weaken: that's the muscle you're training.
step22.title: Three voices — at the end
step22.why: You will see whether reassuring grew and harshness and dislike eased.

step23.intro: Write a letter to yourself for a worse day, in the voice of your compassionate self. It returns in the week you choose.
step23.title: Letter for a worse day
step23.why: Worse days will come back. A letter from a good day works when warmth toward yourself is just missing.

step24.intro: Decide which practices stay with you and in what rhythm. This step closes the path; the Return comes in eight weeks.
step24.title: What stays with me
step24.why: Without a decision the practices fade. You choose a few that stay and a rhythm that will hold.

step25.intro: The Return after eight weeks: the self-compassion scale for the fourth time.
step25.title: Self-compassion — eight weeks on
step25.why: The fourth measure tells what held without the path.

step26.intro: The Return: the three voices for the third time.
step26.title: Three voices — eight weeks on
step26.why: The third measure of the voices: what remained of what was practised.

step27.intro: Read the letter from yourself. What stayed, what came back, one small move for the coming week.
step27.title: What stayed, what came back
step27.why: The return is not an exam. It is a look at what helps day to day and one small move further.

paced-breathing.intro: Every day for the first two weeks, from day one. Two or three minutes of exhaling longer than you inhale. The foundation for everything that follows; after the compassionate self, the self-compassion break takes over.

moment-shame.intro: Every other day from the shame map to the end of the critic work. Five taps: which part took the wheel, when you noticed, what you did instead, how strong. The rest is optional. Afterwards Moments stay on demand.

self-compassion-break.intro: Every other day, from the compassionate self to the end of the path. Twenty seconds of breath and three steps: mindfulness, common humanity, kindness.

shame-writing.intro: Every other day in the week of the new voice. After a moment of shame, three paragraphs: common humanity, kindness to yourself, distance. From research: this writing lowers shame-proneness when it's longer than a note.

positive-data-log.intro: Every other day from the beliefs step. You add evidence for the fair demand on yourself.

nameShame.title: Name the shame the moment it appears
nameShame.why: Naming an emotion takes some of its force.

catchBody.title: Catch shame from the body's signal, before a thought names it
catchBody.why: The body is faster than the critic. An early signal buys time for a response.

soothingGesture.title: In a moment of shame, put a hand on your heart or belly and take two calm breaths
soothingGesture.why: Warm touch and a longer exhale calm the threat system faster than thoughts do.

receiveKindness.title: Receive kindness from someone without deflecting it
receiveKindness.why: Compassion from others is an easier flow than compassion for yourself. Received, it teaches the body that warmth is safe.

title.m: After a hard moment, do for yourself what you'd do for a friend
title.f: After a hard moment, do for yourself what you'd do for a friend

kindAct.why: Compassion is practised through action, not only words.

useResponse.title: Use your shame response when shame shows up
useResponse.why: The plan only works once you use it in the heat of the moment. Every attempt counts, even a late one.

unblendSay.title: In a moment of shame, tell yourself: that's my part, not me
unblendSay.why: Unblending leaves someone in you who can hear the part out and stay.

friendTest.title: At one moment of shame, ask: should someone close to me, in my place, be ashamed of this?
friendTest.why: If not, it's someone else's demand. The question takes its power away.

stayLonger.title: Stay in the situation a minute longer instead of withdrawing
stayLonger.why: Shame says disappear. A minute longer shows nothing happens.

repairGuilt.title: At one situation of guilt, make a real repair
repairGuilt.why: Guilt closes through repair, shame through hiding. Choose repair.

noticeCritic.title: Notice the critic's voice and call it by its name
noticeCritic.why: A named critic is a part, not the truth about you.

handOver.title: Thank the critic and tell it you're taking the wheel
handOver.why: The critic protects. Thanks relieves it of guard duty without a fight.

sayNo.title: Say one "no" without explaining yourself
sayNo.why: The fierce side of compassion: a boundary set without apology tells the body you have the right to take up space.

readAloud.title: Say one sentence from your letter out loud
readAloud.why: A sentence spoken aloud is heard by the body too. Read silently, it stays in the head.

defendSelf.title: Use your defending sentence when the critic attacks
defendSelf.why: The hated self doesn't weaken from warmth alone. It also needs someone to say "enough".

collectEvidence.title: Catch evidence for the fair demand in daily life
collectEvidence.why: The task is noticing. The note goes into the positive data log.

breakDemand.title: Do one thing that someone else's demand forbids
breakDemand.why: A demand weakens when you break it and nothing bad happens. That's your experiment.

tellSafePerson.title: Tell one safe person about something you're ashamed of
tellSafePerson.why: Being seen by someone kind is what works best on shame.

showImperfect.title: Show up imperfectly in a small situation
showImperfect.why: Unfinished work or admitting "I don't know" is a small exposure to being seen.

askQuestion.title: Ask a question that feels "stupid"
askQuestion.why: Not knowing is the most common borrowed demand. A question breaks it in ten seconds.

keepResponse.title: Use your shame response without a reminder from the app
keepResponse.why: A habit is when the plan comes by itself.

title.m: Ask for support with something you usually handle alone
title.f: Ask for support with something you usually handle alone

askSupport.why: Shame isolates. Asking for help is a move in the opposite direction.

shame-compassion.goal: Notice shame sooner. Answer with warmth, to yourself and to others, instead of attack or hiding. Return to contact.

ifs-parts.title: Meet your parts
ifs-parts.description: A four-week IFS path: from a parts map, through unblending, trailheads and protector appreciation, to a dialogue with a part — and at the end, if the protectors allow it, a short exile witnessing. A daily IFS check-in alongside the steps is worth it.

step1.intro: Start with a map: gather the parts you already know and see how they relate to each other.

step2.intro: A short unblending practice — notice the part that carries you away and take a step back into Self.

step3.intro: Follow a trailhead: a strong reaction from recent days is a trail leading to a part.

step4.intro: Self-energy check-in (the 8 C’s) — see how much calm, curiosity and compassion you have day to day. This is hygiene, not a finale.

step5.intro: Appreciate a protector — learn its job and its fear before asking for deeper access.

step6.intro: Talk with the part that needs your attention most — writing both sides of the dialogue.

step7.intro: Optional step: be with a younger part for a moment, without fixing and without the whole story — only if the protectors agree. If they say “not yet”, that is an answer too.

cbt-thoughts.title: CBT: thoughts under the lens
cbt-thoughts.description: Learn the cognitive distortions, practice the thought record over a few rounds and descend to the core beliefs beneath them.

step1.intro: Theory in practice first: learn to recognize the common cognitive distortions.

step2.intro: Your first thought record — catch a hot thought and work it through step by step.

step3.intro: Second round: the thought record works best as a regular practice.

step4.intro: An optional third round — consolidate the habit before going deeper.

step5.intro: The finale: from single thoughts to the core beliefs that feed them.

outcomeQuestion.f: How did this task go? What turned out differently than you expected?

maintenance.lead: Each gets a next date ({rhythm}) and offers the next one once done, like every repeat.

dose.title: Is it too much?

leadTooMuch.m: You wrote that the practices are too much. Less often works too — regularity counts, not quantity.
leadTooMuch.f: You wrote that the practices are too much. Less often works too — regularity counts, not quantity.

leadNone.m: You wrote that you are not doing them. No reproach. Let us keep only the smallest thing: the breath. The rest once a week, until there is room again.
leadNone.f: You wrote that you are not doing them. No reproach. Let us keep only the smallest thing: the breath. The rest once a week, until there is room again.

followUp.reenrollDescription: A second round tends to differ from the first: you know the steps, so more attention goes to what happens. Staying with what helps is fine too.
